# A finite cap-band barrier for simultaneous unique-corner losses

This note proves a finite, rather than infinitesimal, preservation theorem for ordinary planar Lorentz rows. It applies to exact fixed-section losses in unique-signature sectors. It does not cover ears, section changes, or a containing triangle whose own cap fractions exceed the stated ceiling.

## 1. Positive raw data and the loss path

For positive k,Q_i,sigma_i, i=1,2,3, define

    q_i=Q_i/k,
    M=sum_i Q_i/sigma_i,
    f_i=2sqrt(k Q_i)/(sigma_i M),
    Phi_i=f_i+(f_j+f_l)^2/4,     {i,j,l}={1,2,3}.

The exact normalization identity is

    sum_i f_i sqrt(q_i)=2.                              (1)

Fix nonnegative losses E_i and write E=sum E_i. Consider the path

    k(t)=k(0)-tE,
    Q_i(t)=Q_i(0)-tE_i,
    sigma_i(t)=sigma_i(0),       0<=t<=1.               (2)

Assume its endpoint data remain positive. Positivity then holds throughout the path. Each ratio q_i(t) is monotone or constant, since its derivative has constant sign. Thus if all cap fractions at BOTH endpoints are at most c, then the same is true along the whole path.

We use the exact ceiling

    c=128/279.

## 2. A strictly inward loss derivative at the common feasible boundary

Fix a selected row i, and suppose at some positive data point that

    Phi_i=2,       Phi_j<=2,       Phi_l<=2,
    q_s<=c for every s.                                (3)

Put x=f_i, g=f_j+f_l, and z=sqrt(2-x). Then g=2z, and

    F=f_1+f_2+f_3=3-(z-1)^2,
    C=x+g^2/2=2+z^2.                                  (4)

Identity (1) implies F>=2/sqrt(c). The exact arithmetic inequality

    4/c-(7379/2500)^2=85093/12500000>0

therefore gives F>7379/2500=3-(11/50)^2. Consequently

    39/50<z<61/50.                                    (5)

For any index s the row inequality Phi_s<=2 can be written, using the common F, as

    [f_s-(F-2)]^2<=4(3-F).                             (6)

Combining (6) for j,l with f_j+f_l=2z yields the following common upper bound on either f_j or f_l:

    f_s <= z^2-2z+2       when z<=1,
    f_s <= 4z-z^2-2       when z>=1.                   (7)

For example, when z<=1 the individual lower bound in (6) is 4z-z^2-2; subtracting it from their sum gives the first line. When z>=1 the upper bound in (6) gives the second line directly. These arguments remain valid if a displayed lower bound is negative; on interval (5) it is positive anyway.

Both bounds in (7) are STRICTLY less than 4z/(2+z^2) on interval (5). Here is an exact polynomial verification. For z<=1, multiply by 2+z^2 and subtract 4z, obtaining

    P_-(z)=z^4-2z^3+4z^2-8z+4.

Its derivative is increasing because P_-''=12z^2-12z+8>0, and P_-'(1)=-2. Hence P_- decreases on [39/50,1], and

    P_-(39/50)=-2408459/6250000<0.

For z>=1 the analogous polynomial is

    P_+(z)=-z^4+4z^3-4z^2+4z-4.

On [1,61/50], its derivative is

    4[1-z(z-1)(z-2)]>0,

while

    P_+(61/50)=-159641/6250000<0.

Thus throughout (5),

    f_j,f_l <4z/(2+z^2)=2g/C.                         (8)

Now differentiate Phi_i under the raw loss of one unit of k and the same unit of Q_s, with all sections fixed. Write

    e_i=f_i=x,
    e_j=g f_j/2,       e_l=g f_l/2.

Direct differentiation gives minus the coefficient

    alpha_s=C/(2k)+e_s/(2Q_s)-C/(M sigma_s).

Using the definition of f_s, this is equivalently

    2k alpha_s=C+e_s T_s^2-C f_s T_s,
    T_s=1/sqrt(q_s)>0.                                (9)

For s=i, completing the square or minimizing over all real T_s gives

    2k alpha_i >= C-x C^2/4
                =C(2-x)^2/4>0.                       (10)

The last strictness uses z>0, so x<2. For s=j,l, the quadratic minimum in (9) gives

    2k alpha_s >= C-C^2 f_s/(2g)>0,                   (11)

where the final inequality is exactly (8). We have proved:

**Boundary loss lemma.** At every data point (3), the derivative of the tight row is strictly negative under any nonzero nonnegative combination of unique-sector losses (2).

No geometric realizability of intermediate data was used in this lemma; it is an exact statement about the positive raw quantities and their normalization.

## 3. Finite preservation, with simultaneous losses

**Theorem.** Assume the positive endpoints of (2) both obey q_i<=128/279, and initially all three rows obey Phi_i<=2. Then all three final rows obey Phi_i<=2. If E>0, all three final rows are strictly below 2.

**Proof.** The cap ceiling holds all along the path by Section 1. At any time when all rows are at most 2 and one row equals 2, its derivative equals

    -sum_s E_s alpha_s<0

when E>0, by Section 2. In particular every initially tight row enters the strict region for sufficiently small positive time, and initially strict rows remain strict by continuity. If some row ever reaches 2 again, take the first such time after this initial strict interval. That row approaches 2 from below and hence has nonnegative left derivative at its first contact. The derivative exists and is strictly negative by the boundary loss lemma, a contradiction. The same argument includes contact at t=1. Thus every row is strict for all positive times. The case E=0 is unchanged data. This proves the theorem without an appeal to an unproved differential-inclusion or invariance result.

## 4. Actual convex-body application

Let K_0,K_1 be planar convex bodies with a common interior source and three fixed balanced spanning normals. Suppose K_1 subset K_0, their three full cutting sections agree, and every point removed from K_0 belongs, up to null boundaries, to one of the three unique-signature regions. Let E_i be the actual removed area in unique sector i. Then their exact raw data satisfy (2) at its endpoints: total area loses sum E_i, only cap i loses E_i, and all section lengths are unchanged.

If both bodies have all three cap fractions at most 128/279 and K_0 satisfies the three Lorentz inequalities, then K_1 does also. The inequalities become strict under any positive area loss.

In particular take a strict distinct-vertex triangle T whose own three cap fractions are at most 128/279. Let C_T be the convex hull of its six cutting-ray endpoints. Every convex K with C_T subset K subset T has the same three sections, and the losses lie in the three disjoint unique corner triangles. If K also satisfies the same cap ceiling, then all its Lorentz rows are at most 2, and strictly below 2 unless K=T. This conclusion allows arbitrary finite corner losses and arbitrarily many vertices or curved corner boundaries; it is not restricted to a sufficiently small Hausdorff or area neighborhood.

The ceiling on the initial containing triangle is essential to this proof. The theorem does not assert that every cap-band quadrilateral admits such a containing triangle. The exact global quadrilateral reduction is a separate result, and the remaining quadrilateral incidence regimes are not resolved here.

## 5. Every double-sector gain has a strictly inward derivative too

Keep the common boundary hypotheses (3). In addition to (5), all three f_s are at least

    f_s>=1279/2500.                                    (12)

For the selected entry this follows from f_i=2-z^2 and z<=61/50. For the others, the lower bound in (6) is 4z-z^2-2 when z<=1, and 2-z^2 when z>=1; its minimum on the two intervals is again 1279/2500. There is no dependence here on which row is selected.

Since sqrt(c)<17/25 and F<=3, identity (1) now gives, for every s,

    sqrt(q_s)>17/25-(1/25)/f_s
             >=17/25-100/1279>3/5.

Indeed the first bound follows by placing the other two cap roots strictly below 17/25, and the last inequality is equivalent to 2558>2500. Also sqrt(q_s)<=sqrt(c)<7/10. Hence

    10/7<T_s=1/sqrt(q_s)<5/3.                          (13)

Add one unit of area to double sector s, which is captured by the two caps other than s. This increases k and those two Q's by one, leaving the third Q and all sections unchanged. Its derivative beta_s satisfies

    2k beta_s=C+sum_(j!=s)[e_j T_j^2-C f_j T_j].        (14)

We prove the uniform strict bound

    beta_s<-1/(4k).                                   (15)

Each summand in (14) is convex as a function of T_j, so (13) reduces upper bounds to its two endpoints 10/7 and 5/3. If s is the selected row i, the two other summands have the same multiplier function, giving the upper bound

    C+2z max_(T in {10/7,5/3})[z T^2-C T].             (16)

If s is not selected, let j be the included nonselected index. Its f_j has the stronger lower bound

    L_-(z)=4z-z^2-2        on 39/50<=z<=1,
    L_+(z)=z^2-2z+2        on 1<=z<=61/50.              (17)

The first line is (6). For the second line subtract the upper bound f_l<=4z-z^2-2 from the sum f_j+f_l=2z. Both are positive on their respective intervals.

For every T in the endpoint pair, zT-C<0: C-zT>=2+z^2-5z/3>0. Also T-C<0. Thus the corresponding upper bound on (14) is

    C+(2-z^2)(T_1^2-C T_1)
                  +L_-(z)(z T_2^2-C T_2),            (18)

on the lower interval, using L_+ on the upper interval, for T_1,T_2 in {10/7,5/3}. All six upper-bound polynomials (16),(18) are strictly below -1/2 on each indicated interval.

Here is a finite rational certificate for that last assertion. For a polynomial P of degree n and an interval [a,b], expand

    -P(a+(b-a)u)=sum_(k=0)^n c_k u^k
               =sum_(j=0)^n B_j binom(n,j)u^j(1-u)^(n-j),
    B_j=sum_(k=0)^j c_k binom(j,k)/binom(n,k).          (19)

The second equality follows by the binomial theorem. The nonnegative Bernstein basis functions sum to one on [0,1]. For the displayed P, the minimum of the B_j is given by the following exact table. Every printed number exceeds 1/2; therefore -P>1/2 throughout each interval.

| Polynomial | Endpoint choices | [39/50,1] minimum | [1,61/50] minimum |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| (16) without max | T=10/7 | 441821/612500 | 73/49 |
| (16) without max | T=5/3 | 4959/6250 | 13/9 |
| (18) | T_1=10/7,T_2=10/7 | 6347669/7656250 | 386711/612500 |
| (18) | T_1=10/7,T_2=5/3 | 3197731/3750000 | 308439211/551250000 |
| (18) | T_1=5/3,T_2=10/7 | 368112407/551250000 | 374439739/551250000 |
| (18) | T_1=5/3,T_2=5/3 | 972313/1406250 | 136669/225000 |

All entries result from the explicitly given coefficient formula (19), with C=2+z^2 and L_- or L_+ as in (17); no numerical approximation or optimization enters the certificate. Equations (16)--(19) prove (15).

## 6. The combined finite sector-transfer theorem

Let E_i>=0 be unique-sector losses, and G_i>=0 be double-sector gains, where double sector i misses cap i. Set E=sum E_i and G=sum G_i. Keep all three sections fixed and consider the exact data path

    k(t)=k(0)+t(G-E),
    Q_i(t)=Q_i(0)+t(G-G_i-E_i),       0<=t<=1.          (20)

Assume positive endpoint data, that both endpoints obey q_i<=128/279, and that all initial Lorentz rows are at most 2. Then all final rows are at most 2; if any E_i or G_i is positive, all final rows are strictly below 2.

Each cap ratio in (20) is monotone or constant, so the ceiling holds throughout. At a common feasible boundary its row derivative is exactly

    -sum_i E_i alpha_i+sum_i G_i beta_i<0

for any nonzero transfer. The unique-loss signs are Sections 1--2, and the double-gain signs are Section 5. The same first-contact argument of Section 3 now proves the assertion. Intermediate data need not be geometrically realizable; positive endpoint data and affine interpolation are sufficient for the purely algebraic barrier.

For actual bodies, this theorem applies whenever they have exactly the same three full sections, the final unique-sector areas do not exceed the initial ones, and its final double-sector areas are no smaller. These are explicit geometric premises. The theorem does not infer them from a volume comparison, or assume that an arbitrary quadrilateral can be reached from a cap-band triangle in this way.

## 7. The lost cap's own row is preserved globally in every dimension

There is a separate statement requiring NO cap ceiling and NO assumptions on other rows. Fix d>=2 and positive data k,Q_i,sigma_i for d+1 indices, and define

    M=sum_i Q_i/sigma_i,
    f_i=d k^(1/d) Q_i^((d-1)/d)/(sigma_i M),
    Phi_s=f_s+(d-1)[(sum_(i!=s) f_i)/d]^(d/(d-1)).

Decrease k and Q_s by the same amount E>0, keeping all other Q_i and all sections fixed, and assume final k and Q_s remain positive. If initially Phi_s<=d, then finally Phi_s<d.

To prove the claim, it suffices to verify a strictly inward derivative at every boundary point Phi_s=d, and then use the same first-contact argument as before. Put x=f_s, so 0<x<d because all other f_i are positive. The sum of the logarithmic derivative weights of this row is

    C=x+[d/(d-1)](d-x)=(d^2-x)/(d-1).

Differentiating under the simultaneous loss and putting T=(Q_s/k)^(-1/d)>0 gives minus a coefficient alpha_s with

    d k alpha_s=C+(d-1)x T^d-Cx T^(d-1).

The last two terms have their global minimum for T>0 at T=C/d. Thus

    d k alpha_s >= C-x(C/d)^d>0.                     (21)

For the final strict inequality, the function

    x[(d^2-x)/(d-1)]^(d-1)

is strictly increasing on 0<x<d: its logarithmic derivative is
1/x-(d-1)/(d^2-x)>0 there. Its value at x=d is d^d. Therefore x C^(d-1)<d^d, exactly the strict inequality in (21). All intermediate data stay positive, and the differentiations are smooth. The first-contact proof consequently gives the finite result.

For an actual convex body this applies, in particular, when a unique region of cap s is removed while all d+1 cutting sections stay unchanged. It controls the row indexed by that cap globally. It does NOT control the other d rows after the same removal, and hence does not by itself prove the full quadrilateral claim in the plane.

For future use the exact planar one-corner path can also retain its true triangle heights. Normalize the initial triangle area to 1, let a_i be its positive vertex-cap heights divided by their sum, so sum a_i=1, and put P_i=a_i^2/q_i. Its original row factors are f_i=2sqrt(P_i). Removing e=q_s r from unique corner s gives

    f_s(r)=2sqrt(P_s) sqrt[(1-q_s r)(1-r)]/(1-a_s r),
    f_j(r)=2sqrt(P_j) sqrt(1-q_s r)/(1-a_s r), j!=s.   (22)

Here the actual loss range and the actual heights a_i remain part of the geometry. Formula (22) follows from the unchanged sections and M(r)=M(0)(1-a_s r). It records the exact dependence that is absent from the scalar profile/floor obstruction; no inequality for the other rows is inferred from it.
